reasons_add: Al-Zajjāj allows accusative rabb al-ʿālamīn in ordinary speech as detached praise with an implied ‘I mention the Lord of the worlds’; he cites an unnamed poet to show that accusative epithets may follow a preceding noun or serve as praise, and says grammarians accept these case combinations.

Al-Zajjāj allows genitive rabb as continuation in ordinary speech and cites an unnamed poet for epithets that follow the preceding noun. He says the Qurʾan chooses the best and most eloquent wording, the genitive sequence rabb al-ʿālamīn al-raḥmān al-raḥīm, despite other case forms being possible in ordinary speech.

Al-Zajjāj explains nominative rabb al-ʿālamīn as ‘He is the Lord of the worlds’; his unnamed poetic example illustrates how nominative epithets may state ‘they are the ones,’ among case combinations accepted by grammarians.
Al-Zajjāj takes al-ʿālamīn to mean everything God created and supports the breadth of ‘Lord of the worlds’ with ‘He is Lord of everything’ (6:164).

Al-Zajjāj reports Sibawayh’s explanation that the plural nūn has fatḥa to distinguish it from the dual nūn with kasra. Al-Zajjāj adds that fatḥa also resolves two adjacent still letters, since kasra after wāw or yāʾ is heavy, and cites sawfa and ayna Zayd as analogies.
Al-Zajjāj says al-ʿālamīn has no singular of its own form because it gathers unlike kinds, whereas a single ʿālam gathers members of one kind.
Al-Zajjāj explicitly calls al-ʿālamīn the plural of ʿālam, distinguishing its gathered kinds from the members grouped in one ʿālam.
Al-Ghazālī, as reported by al-Biqāʿī, takes the Fātiḥa’s repeated mercy as pointing to perfect creation and provision for each world, alongside mercy in the afterlife.
ʿAlī counts the basmala as a verse when challenged that al-Ḥamd has only six verses; Abū Hurayra reports a seven-verse count that expressly includes the basmala.
Abū Hurayra reports the title Fātiḥat al-Kitāb among the names of the seven-verse sūra.
ʿAlī calls the seven oft-repeated al-Ḥamd, identifying the sūra by its opening praise.

Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet calling ‘Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds’ the Mother of the Qurʾan and the Mother of the Book; another report from Abū Hurayra includes Mother of the Qurʾan among the Fātiḥa’s titles.

Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet calling the opening praise the seven oft-repeated; ʿAlī identifies them as al-Ḥamd and counts the basmala to make seven; another report from Abū Hurayra gives the title alongside a seven-verse count that includes the basmala.

question: 1:2/q18
position: The Fātiḥa’s repeated mercy links provision for every world to mercy in the afterlife.
reasons: Al-Ghazālī, as reported by al-Biqāʿī, reads its repeated mercy as signaling perfect creation and provision for each world together with mercy in the afterlife.

question: What recitation follows completion of the Qurʾān in Ibn Kathīr’s practice?

positions.position: After the final takbīr, recite the Fātiḥa, the first five verses of al-Baqara, and the completion supplication.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, as reported by Ibn al-Jazarī in al-Nashr, says Ibn Kathīr’s takbīr begins after al-Ḍuḥā and continues at each sūra through al-Nās; after its final takbīr come the Fātiḥa, al-Baqara through 2:5, and the completion supplication. He calls this al-ḥāl al-murtaḥil.
